resources.string: Hip attachments
Right gluteus maximus from behind, with its origins on the pelvis and two insertions at the lateral hip.
Iliac origin
Upper fibers arise along the posterior gluteal line and the adjacent outer surface of the ilium.
Sacral origin
Medial fibers arise from the back of the sacrum and the side of the coccyx. Other fibers arise from the nearby sacrotuberous ligament.
Iliotibial tract
The upper fibers blend into the iliotibial tract, a thickened strip of fascia that continues down the outside of the thigh.
Gluteal tuberosity
The lowest fibers attach to the gluteal tuberosity, a roughened ridge on the back of the upper femur below the greater trochanter.
Calf attachments
Right gastrocnemius from behind, from the two origins above the knee to the shared tendon at the heel.
Medial head origin
The medial head starts at the back of the femur just above the medial condyle. Its muscle belly forms the inner bulge of the calf.
Lateral head origin
The lateral head starts just above the lateral femoral condyle and forms the outer bulge of the calf.
Calf aponeurosis
Fibers from both heads attach to a broad tendinous sheet. It narrows and joins the soleus contribution to form the Achilles tendon.
Calcaneal insertion
The Achilles tendon carries both gastrocnemius heads and the soleus to the back of the calcaneal tuberosity, the prominent part of the heel bone.
Tendon cross-section
Achilles tendon in place and an enlarged schematic cross-section showing how collagen bundles are organized.
Achilles tendon
This segment of the Achilles tendon lies below the calf muscle bellies and above the heel attachment. The enlarged view looks across the tendon, rather than along it.
Epitenon
The epitenon is the thin connective tissue layer immediately around the tendon proper. It forms the rim of the enlarged section.
Collagen fascicle
A fascicle is a bundle of smaller collagen fibers that run mainly along the tendon. In cross-section, bundles appear as separate profiles.
Endotenon
This connective tissue runs between neighboring fascicles and separates their collagen bundles. It appears as narrow channels in the cross-section.
